transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2025-11-20
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE); Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE); Ravi Patel (CTO, Polaris AI); Emily Stone (ML Eng Lead); Jordan Lee (Infra); Tamara Fox (Procurement)

Summary: Quick discovery focused on cost/unit economics for hosted vs dedicated vs private deployments. Polaris has a constrained monthly budget target and needs clarity on per-token cost levers (batching, KV/prefix caching, quantization) and the tradeoffs for latency vs unit cost.

Topics: pricing, batching/caching levers, dedicated sizing, private deployment constraints, security docs/SOC2, benchmarking next steps

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone good afternoon, um we wanted to focus today on cost levers and which deployment makes the most sense for you all, quick intros?
[00:12] Ravi Patel: Yeah hi I'm Ravi CTO at Polaris. We're building an embeddings + chat assistant for enterprise search. Our primary constraints are monthly spend—roughly target is around $100k per month for inference—and latency SLOs under 300ms tail for search.
[00:30] Emily Stone: Emily here, ML lead. We'll be using a 16k context model for assistant and 2k for embeddings, and a lot of short requests but heavy burstiness at 10am daily.
[00:45] Diego Alvarez: Got it. Diego from Redwood SE, I work on performance and benchmarking. So quick high-level: hosted API is easiest (pay-as-you-go), dedicated is reserved capacity with better unit pricing and SLOs, private is for VPC/on-prem for regulatory needs. We'll walk through per-token math.
[01:05] Ravi Patel: Sounds good. We're trying to understand where batching and caching actually move the needle vs just buying more capacity.
[01:14] Maya Chen: Perfect question. I'll hand to Diego to explain the key levers and then we can map it to your budget.
[01:20] Diego Alvarez: Sure. So three main levers: 1) batching—amortizes compute across requests, 2) prefix/KV cache—avoids re-computing common prompt prefixes, 3) quantization/model variant—INT8/4-bit variants reduce GPU memory and cost. For hosted, you get automatic batching and caching heuristics; for dedicated you can tune batch size and cache allocation per model.
[01:41] Emily Stone: Uh when you say automatic batching in hosted, is there any risk to latency? We're sensitive to tail latency.
[01:48] Diego Alvarez: Good callout. Hosted aims for sub-100ms added latency for typical requests, but bursty workloads can increase queue times. For strict tail SLOs you can use Dedicated with reserved throughput and configure max batch wait (we set tight thresholds to meet 300ms tails). There's a tradeoff: larger batches lower cost per token but increase latency.
[02:10] Ravi Patel: Can you show some concrete per-token numbers? Like for embeddings vs chat generation.
[02:15] Maya Chen: Sure — I'll share a quick example, and then we'll send the sheet after. Rough ballpark: hosted generation cost ranges (model dependent) e.g. $0.0006 to $0.002 per input+output token for 16k models on on-demand; embeddings around $0.0002/token. Dedicated reserved pricing can drop per-token compute cost by ~30-50% depending on commit and batch configuration. But you trade off commit and minimum monthly.
[02:39] Jordan Lee: That 30-50% is compute-only right? What about operational overheads like network egress and S3 storage?
[02:46] Diego Alvarez: Correct, compute. Network egress follows cloud provider pricing where applicable; we include a breakdown in the pricing sheet. Also for Dedicated we include a predictable per-hour node cost so you can forecast.
[03:00] Emily Stone: On batching—do you have any heuristics for when batch size helps vs hurts for short, often single-turn prompts like ours?
[03:08] Diego Alvarez: Yes—if you have many concurrent single-turn prompts, batching helps a lot. For highly conversational workloads with long KV cache hits, caching helps more. We typically recommend batching window of 20-50ms for low-latency services; for throughput-oriented backfills you can use 100-200ms to maximize batch fill.
[03:27] Ravi Patel: Okay so if we optimize prompts and use prefix caching, how much can we expect per-token reduction? Like percent?
[03:34] Diego Alvarez: It depends on prompt redundancy. Typical prefix caching savings range from 10% up to 60% for highly templated prompts. For embeddings, less beneficial. Combined with batching you might see overall cost/unit reductions of 30-60% on Dedicated vs naive hosted on-demand.
[03:50] Tamara Fox: From procurement side we're also watching contractual minimums—what's a typical committed monthly for Dedicated?
[03:57] Maya Chen: Commit levels vary; many customers start with a $20k–$50k/month commit for Dedicated to secure better pricing tiers and predictable capacity. If your target is $100k/month, that fits well with a mid-level dedicated tier.
[04:12] Ravi Patel: We are also considering Private (VPC) because of data residency—what's the delta vs Dedicated in cost and ops?
[04:20] Diego Alvarez: Private includes the Dedicated runtime but with customer-managed networking and additional enterprise licensing. There's typically a platform fee for Private and possible integration/engineering costs upfront. Unit compute costs are similar to Dedicated, but the total cost of ownership is higher initially because of setup and potential on-prem infra.
[04:36] Emily Stone: When you say quantization variants—do you have benchmarks on quality drop for 4-bit vs full FP16 for our 16k model?
[04:44] Diego Alvarez: We do internal benchmarks—quality delta is small for many tasks but depends on your eval sets. We recommend doing a small eval on your prompts; that's something we can run in the benchmarking engagement. Quantization plus KV cache often yields large cost wins with minimal quality loss for retrieval-augmented assistants.
[05:05] Ravi Patel: For budgeting let's run a quick hypothetical: 500M tokens/month, mostly generation, and 100M embedding tokens. What does that look like?
[05:13] Maya Chen: High level: if hosted on-demand averages $0.001/token for generate, 500M -> $500k (compute only), embeddings at $0.0002 -> $20k, total $520k. With Dedicated + batching/caching/quantization you could get to ~$250k–$350k depending on efficiency—so big savings but requires commit.
[05:36] Tamara Fox: That delta is significant. Our internal budget target is $100k/month so we need a plan to get there or reduce token consumption.
[05:45] Emily Stone: Could we offload some workloads to cheaper model variants for non-critical queries? Like smaller embedding models or cheaper generation models?
[05:52] Diego Alvarez: Absolutely—routing by policy is recommended. Redwood supports model variants and fallbacks; you can route low-cost queries to smaller models and high-value ones to high-quality models. That often shuts down a big portion of cost.
[06:05] Jordan Lee: For the benchmarking run, what env do you need from us? VPC peering? sample prompts?
[06:10] Diego Alvarez: We'll need sample workload (prompts + distribution), expected concurrency, AWS/GCP account role for dedicated trial if you want to test Dedicated in your VPC, or we can run on our hosted infra with your data redacted. Also required: list of models to test and success criteria—e.g., 95th percentile latency < 300ms and cost per 1k tokens <$X.
[06:30] Ravi Patel: On security docs—SOC2 and KMS—how is key management handled for Private vs Hosted?
[06:36] Maya Chen: For Hosted, Redwood manages keys but supports customer-managed KMS for certain enterprise plans. Dedicated in customer VPC can integrate with your KMS. Private (on-prem/VPC) gives you full control over keys and audit logs. We'll share SOC2/ISO docs and the network diagram.
[06:55] Emily Stone: One more question on caching—does the KV cache persist across model versions or rollouts?
[07:00] Diego Alvarez: Good question—cache persists per model variant unless you opt to rehydrate strategy during rollouts. We have tools to warm caches during canary and A/B to avoid cold-start cost spikes.
[07:15] Tamara Fox: Procurement needs to know lead time for Dedicated and Private deployments—what's typical?
[07:20] Maya Chen: Dedicated provisioning is usually days to a couple weeks depending on commit and region. Private onboarding (esp on-prem) can take weeks to months depending on network and compliance work. We'll include an estimated timeline in the follow-up.
[07:33] Ravi Patel: For our $100k/month goal—any tactical suggestions to get there fast?
[07:38] Diego Alvarez: Tactically: 1) Enable prompt templating + prefix caching ASAP, 2) Route low-value queries to smaller models, 3) Use Dedicated reserved capacity with aggressive batching for non-interactive workloads, 4) Quantize where acceptable. Also we can run a 1-week benchmark to measure realistic savings before you commit.
[07:55] Emily Stone: Could you also show an example of per-request accounting? Like token counts, batch fill, effective cost per request?
[08:02] Diego Alvarez: Yes we'll add a worked example in the pricing sheet showing per-request token math and effective cost given batch fill rates.
[08:12] Maya Chen: Okay let's recap and assign next steps. Diego will own the benchmark proposal and sizing; I'll send the pricing and security docs. Ravi/Emily to share sample prompts and traffic profile. Jordan to share network contacts for VPC if we go that route.
[08:28] Ravi Patel: Sounds good. One last quick clarifying thing: if we do Dedicated, is there an option to burst to hosted for spikes?
[08:35] Diego Alvarez: Yes we support hybrid routing—Dedicated primary with fallback to hosted or lower-cost regions. That's part of the reliability playbook.
[08:44] Tamara Fox: From contracting perspective, do you allow quarterly commit trials?
[08:49] Maya Chen: We have flexible pilots—often month-to-month pilots that convert to committed tiers after evaluation. We'll outline options in the pricing doc.
[08:59] Emily Stone: Great. I'll get the prompt set over by end of Friday.
[09:03] Maya Chen: Perfect. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the materials and calendar invites for the benchmark kickoff.
[09:10] Ravi Patel: Thanks, bye.

End of transcript.
